newsitem.title: LEBANON: De Charette warns of worsening Mideast tension.
newsitem.headline: De Charette warns of worsening Mideast tension.

text.p: France warned on Thursday that fighting between Moslem guerrillas and Israeli troops in south Lebanon could worsen if Middle East peace talks were not revived immediately.

However, "big obstacles" still blocked the resumption of negotiations, French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said during a stopover in Beirut after talks with Israeli and Syrian leaders during a three-day Middle East tour.
"The situation of stalled peace talks is dangerous for everyone and it presents risks of a deterioration in south Lebanon," de Charette told reporters.
"I firmly say that it is impossible to stay in this situation which presents risks for everyone. The peace process should be relaunched. It is an urgent necessity," he said.
He arrived in Beirut for a brief visit from Damascus after visits to Syria and Israel during which he had talks with Syrian President Hafez al-Assad and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"There remain obstacles which separate the different parties. These obstacles are big," de Charette said after meeting his Lebanese counterpart Faris Bouez.
Israel's Likud government has rejected the land-for-peace formula pursued by the previous Labour government and says it is ready to resume talks with no preconditions.

Syria says the previous Israeli government agreed to hand back the Golan Heights captured in 1967 and talks should resume where they were broken off in February 1996 after a series of bombings in Israel by Palestinian militants.

Fighting between Moslem guerrillas and Israeli troops occupying a south Lebanon border strip has killed two Lebanese civilians, five Israeli soldiers and five Hizbollah (Party of God) guerrillas this year. Another 73 Israeli soldiers died last month in a helicopter collision on their way to south Lebanon.

Lebanon and Israel have repeatedly complained to a five-nation monitoring committee against breaches of an April 26, 1996, ceasefire understanding that ended a 17-day Israeli blitz on Hizbollah in which 200 people, mainly civilians, were killed.

Asked about the efficiency of the group, de Charette said: "The monitoring group is doing day after day, week after week a good job. When we created the monitoring group, we were conscious that it was not enough to create peace. We need to have negotiations to have peace".
The pro-Iranian Hizbollah guerrillas are trying to drive the Israelis and their local militia allies from the 15-km (nine miles)-wide buffer zone.
